Atherosclerosis

Mouse and rabbit experiments report smaller plaque burden or favorable lipid changes, and mouse macrophage assays show greater cholesterol efflux. A rat study combined laser with ultrasound, so its contribution cannot be attributed to light alone.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Mouse and rabbit experiments report lower plaque burden or favorable lipid changes, and mouse macrophage assays show greater cholesterol efflux. A rat study combined laser with ultrasound, so the animal findings do not establish a treatment effect in people.

Summary of the Evidence

Light exposure has been associated with changes in plaque and lipid measures in mouse and rabbit models. The macrophage results suggest a possible cholesterol-handling mechanism. A separate rat experiment combined laser and ultrasound, so the contribution of light cannot be isolated.

Human and clinical evidence

The available research does not include a clinical PBM treatment study in people with atherosclerosis. Reported outcomes concern experimental plaque area, blood lipids, or cell cholesterol handling rather than heart attacks, strokes, symptoms, or revascularization.

Animal evidence

In ApoE-deficient mice fed a Western diet for 18 weeks, daily laser PBM during the final ten weeks was associated with a smaller average aortic plaque area and higher HDL cholesterol than in untreated mice (Yin et al. 2021).

A rabbit study tested polarized-light treatment during a high-cholesterol diet. The longer daily exposure was associated with lower cholesterol and LDL and less atheromatous plaque than in untreated high-cholesterol animals (Park et al. 2012).

A rat study combined ultrasound and laser for metabolic outcomes. Since light was not tested alone, the contribution of PBM cannot be isolated (Paolillo et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The mouse study also tested primary macrophages. The cells showed greater ABCA1 expression and cholesterol efflux and less foam-cell formation under the reported conditions. These experiments help explain the animal findings but are part of the same study, not separate patient evidence (Yin et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The animal studies used different models and interventions: laser PBM in ApoE-deficient mice, polarized light in rabbits, and combined ultrasound and laser in rats. Their wavelengths, routes, and doses should not be treated as one standardized protocol. No head-to-head or dose-finding study identifies an optimal setting for atherosclerosis.

Interpretation

The mouse and rabbit experiments report favorable changes in plaque or lipid measures. Macrophage findings in the mouse study suggest a possible cholesterol-efflux mechanism, while the rat study cannot separate the effects of laser from ultrasound. These findings do not establish reduced cardiovascular events in people.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for a clinical effect in people. The evidence comes from animal models using different interventions; one experiment combined laser with ultrasound.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

All reported outcomes were measured in animal models or macrophages. The mouse and rabbit studies tested different light approaches, and the rat experiment combined laser with ultrasound, so its effects cannot be attributed to light alone. These plaque, lipid, and cell findings do not show whether treatment changes patient outcomes (Yin et al. 2021; Park et al. 2012; Paolillo et al. 2021).
